contraindications: Valproate: hepatic disease (AST 186, bilirubin 2.4, INR 1.6) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 98); risk of hepatotoxicity and bleeding; avoid.
interactions: Lorazepam, midazolam or diazepam + phenobarbital: additive respiratory depression and hypotension; airway and ventilatory support must be available.
Diazepam and midazolam in liver disease: oxidative hepatic metabolism is impaired and their effect is prolonged; lorazepam (glucuronidation) is less affected.
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + amlodipine: additive hypotension during IV loading; induction lowers amlodipine levels. Low albumin (3.0) raises the free phenytoin fraction.
Levetiracetam + current medications: no clinically relevant interaction; no hepatic metabolism.
Thiamine + other drugs: no clinically relevant interaction.

output.query: Status epilepticus in alcohol withdrawal with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy: thiamine and antiseizure treatment

results.finding: Every patient in status epilepticus has a point-of-care glucose; hypoglycemia is treated with IV dextrose, with IV thiamine given first or together where alcohol misuse or malnutrition is suspected.

Wernicke encephalopathy is diagnosed clinically when two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction and altered mental state or memory impairment are present; MRI supports the diagnosis.
Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with IV thiamine, 200 mg three times daily or more, before any carbohydrate, continued until there is no further improvement.
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine; IM midazolam is effective without IV access.

output.summary: Glucose is checked in every patient in status epilepticus and hypoglycemia corrected with dextrose, with thiamine first or together where alcohol misuse is suspected [Brophy_2012]. Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with IV thiamine, at least 200 mg three times daily [EFNS_Wernicke_2010]. Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment of convulsive status epilepticus [Glauser_2016].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 54 low; magnesium 0.8, potassium 2.8 and phosphate 1.6 low; AST 186 over ALT 72, GGT 842, bilirubin 2.4, INR 1.6, platelets 98, MCV 108; ammonia 38 normal; lactate 9.2 with pH 7.16; blood alcohol undetectable, drug screen negative; thiamine 22 low
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, ammonia, coagulation, toxicology
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; ammonia and coagulation follow the alcohol-related liver injury, and toxicology the first seizure in a heavy drinker [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two sets drawn before antimicrobials: no growth to date

action_criteria.rationale: Fever 39.2 C with leukocytosis in a malnourished heavy drinker keeps bacteremia and aspiration open, although withdrawal and prolonged convulsions also raise temperature [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No hemorrhage, subdural collection, contusion or fracture; diffuse cerebral and vermian volume loss
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP; multiple bruises from falls raise subdural hematoma [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous generalized 2-3 Hz spike-and-wave time-locked to the convulsions, with excess beta between discharges
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm ongoing seizures and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Convulsions continuing after midazolam need EEG confirmation of ongoing seizure activity and of its control, since convulsive SE may continue as non-convulsive SE; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Symmetric T2/FLAIR signal in the medial thalami, mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray with medial thalamic restricted diffusion and mammillary enhancement
action_criteria.label: MRI brain for Wernicke encephalopathy and a structural cause of a first SE
action_criteria.rationale: A first SE in a malnourished heavy drinker needs MRI for a structural cause and for the diencephalic signal changes that support Wernicke encephalopathy [Brophy_2012; EFNS_Wernicke_2010].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cell count, protein and glucose ratio; Gram stain, culture and HSV PCR negative
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture after CT: fever 39.2 C with a first SE in a heavy drinker
action_criteria.rationale: Fever with a first SE in a patient at risk of bacterial meningitis makes CNS infection a must-exclude once CT excludes mass effect; platelets 98 are adequate, and the INR of 1.6 from liver injury is corrected to the local LP threshold first [Tunkel_2008; Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate excluded by the liver disease and low platelets; diazepam and midazolam prolonged in liver disease; phenobarbital adds respiratory depression to benzodiazepines; levetiracetam without relevant interaction
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check for the second-line ASM in alcohol-related liver disease
action_criteria.rationale: Liver injury, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia and amlodipine bear on the benzodiazepine and the second-line drug [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on glucose and thiamine in SE and on Wernicke treatment
action_criteria.label: Literature: SE in alcohol withdrawal and Wernicke encephalopathy
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give dextrose without thiamine in this malnourished heavy drinker, and do not delay dextrose to wait for thiamine.
Do not treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy with a 100 mg prophylactic thiamine dose.
Do not use valproate: alcohol-related liver injury with INR 1.6 and platelets 98.
Do not rely on phenytoin or fosphenytoin: it does not control alcohol withdrawal seizures.
required_recommendations: Seizures continue after midazolam 10 mg IM: obtain IV or intraosseous access and give one further benzodiazepine dose (IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg), and load the second-line ASM without delay [Glauser_2016].
Give IV dextrose for glucose 54 mg/dL now, with IV thiamine given first or at the same time; do not delay the dextrose for thiamine [Brophy_2012].

Treat Wernicke encephalopathy with high-dose IV thiamine before or with any carbohydrate: at least 200 mg three times daily [EFNS_Wernicke_2010], commonly 500 mg three times daily for 2 to 3 days, then 250 mg daily.

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), or phenobarbital 15 to 20 mg/kg IV with airway support; avoid valproate because of the liver injury, INR 1.6 and platelets 98, and fosphenytoin, which does not control alcohol withdrawal seizures [ESETT_2019; Brophy_2012].
Replace magnesium (0.8 mg/dL), potassium (2.8 mEq/L) and phosphate (1.6 mg/dL) intravenously, magnesium first, with cardiac monitoring.
Admit to an ICU with airway protection; continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
After seizure control, treat alcohol withdrawal with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines and arrange addiction care before discharge.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Alcohol withdrawal status epilepticus with Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency)

key_clinical_evidence: Alcohol withdrawal seizures peak 6 to 48 hours after the last drink; this SE began at about 36 hours
In malnourished heavy drinkers thiamine is given with or before glucose, without delaying glucose for hypoglycemia
Wernicke encephalopathy needs high-dose IV thiamine; 100 mg is a prophylactic dose
Hypoglycemia, hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia contribute and are corrected at once
Liver injury with coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia excludes valproate; phenytoin does not control withdrawal seizures

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wilson is a 58-year-old man with severe chronic alcohol use disorder who is brought by ambulance in active status epilepticus. His neighbor, who checks on him regularly, called 911 when she found him convulsing on his front porch. She estimates she last saw him drinking 36 hours ago and that he had been trying to quit drinking this week after a conversation with his brother. He had no prior diagnosed epilepsy. He arrived by ambulance with continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 20 minutes. Paramedics noted multiple old bruises from probable falls. No IV access was obtained by EMS due to poor venous access — midazolam 10 mg IM was given without termination of seizures. He is a chronic heavy drinker with 10+ drinks daily for 20 years. He has a malnourished appearance.
